questions.question: Define the term social media influencer / [CO1, CO2, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Define the term social media influencer
  • • A social media influencer is an individual who has built a significant and engaged following on social media
  • platforms and has the power to affect the purchasing decisions or opinions of their audience
  • • Influencers operate across niches — lifestyle, fashion, technology, journalism — and are categorised as mega,
  • macro, micro, or nano based on follower count
  • • Brands collaborate with influencers for product promotion, brand awareness, and audience engagement due
  • to their perceived authenticity and relatability

questions.question: What is meant by video editing techniques?

• What is meant by video editing techniques?

  • motion graphics, and speed control to shape raw footage into a coherent narrative
  • • Techniques such as jump cuts, cross-cutting, and montage are used to control pacing and storytelling flow
  • • Advanced techniques include green screen compositing, text overlays, and visual effects that enhance
  • production value for digital and social media content

questions.question: How does social media content creation differ from traditional media content production?
questions.solution_html:
• How does social media content creation differ from traditional media content production?
  • • Social media content is created for specific platforms with format constraints — short videos, image
  • carousels, stories — whereas traditional media content follows established broadcast or print formats with
  • longer production cycles
  • • Social media production is faster, often real-time, requiring minimal equipment and enabling solo creation;
  • traditional media involves multi-person teams and structured workflows
  • • Social media content prioritises engagement, shareability, and algorithmic performance, while traditional
  • media focuses on editorial depth, broadcast reach, and scheduled delivery

questions.question: Explain challenges in interpreting social media data.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain challenges in interpreting social media data.
  • • Data overload makes it difficult to identify which metrics are truly meaningful for specific campaign
  • objectives, leading to misinterpretation of performance
  • • Vanity metrics such as likes and follower counts may not accurately reflect genuine audience engagement or
  • business impact
  • • Platform algorithm changes, bot activity, and inconsistent data definitions across different platforms further
  • complicate accurate and comparative data interpretation

questions.question: Discuss the role of social media in transforming communication patterns in modern society. / [CO1, CO2, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the role of social media in transforming communication patterns in modern society.
  • • Social media has shifted communication from one-to-many broadcast models to many-to-many interactive
  • networks, democratising information production and distribution
  • • Real-time communication, citizen journalism, and viral content have disrupted traditional gatekeeping roles
  • of editors and broadcasters
  • • Social media has transformed personal communication through instant messaging, community building, and
  • cross-border connectivity
  • • It has introduced new communication formats — stories, reels, threads — that prioritise brevity, visuals, and
  • immediacy over long-form depth
  • • Challenges include misinformation, echo chambers, algorithmic filtering, and erosion of privacy in networked
  • communication environments

questions.question: Discuss the major milestones in the evolution of social media, highlighting the contributions of earlier platforms / [CO1, CO2, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the major milestones in the evolution of social media, highlighting the contributions of earlier
  • platforms
  • • Early platforms like Six Degrees (1997) and Friendster (2002) introduced the concept of online social
  • networking and user profiles
  • • MySpace (2003) popularised personalised profiles and music sharing; LinkedIn (2003) established
  • professional networking as a distinct social media category
  • • Facebook (2004) redefined scale and social connectivity; YouTube (2005) democratised video publishing;
  • Twitter (2006) introduced microblogging and real-time public discourse
  • • Instagram (2010) and Snapchat (2011) shifted focus to visual and ephemeral content; WhatsApp transformed
  • private group communication globally
  • • The rise of TikTok (2016) and short-form video content marked the current era, with algorithm-driven
  • discovery replacing follower-based content distribution

questions.question: Explain the concept of scheduling tools and their importance in digital media management. / [CO3, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the concept of scheduling tools and their importance in digital media management.
  • • Scheduling tools such as Buffer, Hootsuite, Later, and Sprout Social allow content creators and managers to
  • plan, queue, and automatically publish social media posts at predetermined times
  • • They enable consistent posting frequency — a key factor in algorithmic reach — without requiring real-time
  • manual publishing
  • • Scheduling tools support multi-platform management from a single dashboard, saving time and ensuring
  • coordinated campaign execution
  • • They provide analytics integration, allowing teams to schedule content at peak audience activity times for
  • maximum engagement
  • • For organisations and agencies managing multiple accounts, scheduling tools are essential for workflow
  • efficiency, team collaboration, and campaign coherence

questions.question: Map out the measurement techniques for campaign effectiveness. / [CO4, CO5] [10x2 = 20]
questions.solution_html:
• Map out the measurement techniques for campaign effectiveness
  • • Reach and Impressions — measuring how many unique users saw the content and how many total times it
  • was displayed across platforms
  • • Engagement metrics — tracking likes, comments, shares, saves, and click-through rates to assess how
  • audiences interacted with campaign content
  • • Conversion tracking — using UTM parameters, pixel tracking, and landing page analytics to measure how
  • many users completed the desired action (purchase, sign-up, download)
  • • Sentiment analysis — evaluating the tone of audience responses and mentions to gauge qualitative
  • perception of the campaign
  • • Return on Investment (ROI) — comparing campaign costs against revenue generated or goal completions to
  • determine overall effectiveness and justify future budget allocation
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026
